Command object structure:

IMPORTANT: The text inside "keystrokes" will be used completely verbatim as keystrokes. Write commands exactly as you want them sent to the terminal:
- You must end every command with a newline (\n) or it will not execute.
- For special key sequences, use tmux-style escape sequences:

The "duration" attribute specifies the number of seconds to wait for the command to complete (default: 1.0) before the next command will be executed. On immediate tasks (e.g., cd, ls, echo, cat) set a duration of 0.1 seconds. On commands (e.g., gcc, find, rustc) set a duration of 1.0 seconds. On slow commands (e.g., make, python3 [long running script], wget [file]) set an appropriate duration as you determine necessary.

It is better to set a smaller duration than a longer duration. It is always possible to wait again if the prior output has not finished, by running {"keystrokes": "", "duration": 10.0} on subsequent requests to wait longer. Never wait longer than 60 seconds; prefer to poll to see intermediate result status.

import pandas as pd
import lightgbm as lgb
import numpy as np

# Load data
print('Loading data...')
train = pd.read_csv('/app/data/train.csv')
val = pd.read_csv('/app/data/val.csv')
test = pd.read_csv('/app/data/test.csv')

# Separate target and features
target_col = 'target'
X_train = train.drop(columns=[target_col])
y_train = train[target_col]
X_val = val.drop(columns=[target_col])
y_val = val[target_col]

# Identify feature types
# num_ features are numeric, bin_ are numeric/binary, cat_ are categorical
cat_features = [col for col in X_train.columns if col.startswith('cat_')]

# LightGBM dataset
dtrain = lgb.Dataset(X_train, label=y_train, categorical_feature=cat_features)
val_set = lgb.Dataset(X_val, label=y_val, reference=dtrain, categorical_feature=cat_features)

# Hyperparameters for regression
params = {
    'objective': 'regression',
    'metric': 'rmse',
    'verbosity': -1,
    'boosting_type': 'gbdt',
    'random_state': 42,
    'learning_rate': 0.05,
    'num_leaves': 31,
    'feature_fraction': 0.8,
    'bagging_fraction': 0.8,
    'bagging_freq': 5,
}

# Train model
print('Training model...')
model = lgb.train(
    params,
    dtrain,
    num_boost_round=2000,
    valid_sets=[dtrain, val_set],
    valid_names=['train', 'valid'],
    callbacks=[lgb.early_stopping(stopping_rounds=50), lgb.log_evaluation(period=100)]
)

# Predict
print('Predicting...')
preds = model.predict(test)

# Save predictions
# Required: single column named 'target', no index
pred_df = pd.DataFrame({'target': preds})
pred_df.to_csv('/app/predictions.csv', index=False)
print('Predictions saved to /app/predictions.csv')
EOF

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingRegressor

# Load data
print('Loading data...')
train = pd.read_csv('/app/data/train.csv')
val = pd.read_csv('/app/data/val.csv')
test = pd.read_csv('/app/data/test.csv')

# Separate target and features
target_col = 'target'
X_train = train.drop(columns=[target_col])
y_train = train[target_col]
X_val = val.drop(columns=[target_col])
y_val = val[target_col]

# HistGradientBoostingRegressor handles NaNs and categorical features (if specified)
# However, since most features are prefixed with num_ and only one is cat_, 
# we can treat everything as numeric or let it handle the single cat_ feature as numeric 
# (which often works fine for small cardinality) or explicitly set it.

# Identify categorical columns
cat_cols = [i for i, col in enumerate(X_train.columns) if col.startswith('cat_')]
categorical_mask = [i in cat_cols for i in range(len(X_train.columns))]

# Model initialization
print('Training model...')
model = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(
    max_iter=1000,
    learning_rate=0.1,
    max_depth=10,
    random_state=42,
    categorical_features=categorical_mask,
    early_stopping=True,
    validation_fraction=0.1, # Internal split if we didn't have a val set
    n_iter_no_change=50
)

# To use the provided val set for early stopping, we can use partial_fit or similar, 
# but HistGradientBoostingRegressor handles internal validation well.
# Given the time and environment, a standard fit on train should be robust.
model.fit(X_train, y_train)

# Predict
print('Predicting...')
preds = model.predict(test)

# Save predictions
pred_df = pd.DataFrame({'target': preds})
pred_df.to_csv('/app/predictions.csv', index=False)
print('Predictions saved to /app/predictions.csv')
EOF
